name: floating-point number as a distinct type from the real
essential_semantics: A finite-precision representation with a declared format, which is not the mathematical real it approximates and for which arithmetic is not associative.
canonical_example: (a + b) + c differs from a + (b + c) in binary64
rationale: Identifying float with real is the foundational conflation of scientific computing and invalidates symbolic rewrites that assume exact arithmetic.

name: declared precision and number format
essential_semantics: The width and format (binary32/64, fixed point, arbitrary precision) is part of the numeric type and affects reproducibility.
canonical_example: computation in binary32 versus binary64
rationale: Precision is a semantic property of a computed result, not an implementation detail, once error bounds are claimed.

name: rounding mode and tie-breaking
essential_semantics: The rounding rule applied is stated (round-to-nearest-even, toward zero) since it changes results and error bounds.
canonical_example: round half to even makes 0.5 round to 0
rationale: Needed for bit-level reproducibility claims and for correct interval arithmetic.

name: machine epsilon and representable range
essential_semantics: The relative spacing of representable numbers, and the finite range with overflow and underflow thresholds.
canonical_example: eps for binary64 is about 2.2e-16
rationale: Every relative error bound is expressed in units of epsilon.

name: overflow, underflow and special values
essential_semantics: Infinities, NaN and subnormals as representable outcomes with defined propagation, distinguished from mathematical infinity and from undefinedness.
canonical_example: 0.0/0.0 yields NaN, which is not the mathematical statement 'undefined'
rationale: Silent NaN propagation converts a definedness failure into a numeric value, hiding the mathematical error.

name: absolute error
essential_semantics: The difference between a computed and an exact quantity, carrying the same units as the quantity.
canonical_example: |xhat - x| <= 1e-6 metres
rationale: Error claims are meaningless unless absolute and relative are distinguished and units are carried.

name: relative error
essential_semantics: Error normalised by the magnitude of the true value, dimensionless and undefined when the true value is zero.
rationale: The zero-denominator case is a genuine partiality that a tolerance-based comparison must handle explicitly.

name: error bound as a quantified statement
essential_semantics: A bound is a universally quantified claim over an input class, with the class and the norm stated, not a single observed discrepancy.
canonical_example: for all x in [0,1], |p(x) - f(x)| <= 1e-4
rationale: An error bound is a theorem about a method; reducing it to an empirical number removes its guarantee.

name: tolerance as an explicit parameter
essential_semantics: Convergence and equality tests carry an explicit tolerance and its type (absolute, relative, or combined); no hidden default is applied silently.
canonical_example: stop when the relative change is below 1e-8
rationale: A hidden tolerance turns a mathematical equality into an undocumented approximate one.

name: conditioning of a problem
essential_semantics: Sensitivity of the output to input perturbation, a property of the problem independent of the algorithm.
rationale: Ill-conditioning explains why a correct algorithm gives a wrong-looking answer; separating it from stability is essential.

name: numerical stability of an algorithm
essential_semantics: A property of a method (backward or forward stability) as distinct from the conditioning of the problem it solves.
canonical_example: Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting is backward stable in practice
rationale: The problem/algorithm split is the core conceptual structure of numerical analysis and is easily conflated.

name: rate and order of convergence
essential_semantics: How fast an iterative or discretised method approaches its limit, with the order and the asymptotic regime stated.
canonical_example: Newton's method converges quadratically near a simple root
rationale: Rates hold only locally or under hypotheses; unqualified rate claims are frequently false.

name: iterative method with a stated stopping rule
essential_semantics: An update rule, an initial value and a termination criterion, where the returned object is an approximation with a status.
canonical_example: iterate until ||x_{k+1} - x_k|| < tol or k > kmax
rationale: Whether the iteration converged is part of the result; returning only the final iterate hides failure.

name: fixed-point iteration and contraction conditions
essential_semantics: Iterating a map with convergence guaranteed only under a contraction or similar condition.
canonical_example: x_{k+1} = g(x_k) converges if g is a contraction
rationale: The condition is what separates a convergent scheme from a divergent one and must be attachable.

name: numerical root finding
essential_semantics: Approximating solutions of f(x) = 0 with bracketing or initial guesses, returning an approximate root with an error indication.
canonical_example: bisection on [a,b] with f(a)f(b) < 0
rationale: A numerical root is not the exact solution set; the difference must be visible.

name: numerical solution of linear systems
essential_semantics: Solving Ax = b as a computation with conditioning-dependent accuracy, distinct from forming A^{-1}.
canonical_example: solve(A, b) rather than inv(A) @ b
rationale: The mathematical statement and its numerical realisation differ; keeping both views is the point of a mathematical IR with backends.

name: numerical integration
essential_semantics: Approximation of an integral with a rule, node count and an error estimate, and with the exact integral still representable.
canonical_example: Gauss-Legendre with n nodes approximates the integral
rationale: Replacing an integral by a quadrature sum without recording the substitution is silent semantic loss.

name: interpolation and its validity region
essential_semantics: Constructing a function through data with the interpolation scheme and the region of validity recorded; extrapolation is a distinct claim.
canonical_example: cubic spline through knots, invalid outside the knot range
rationale: Silent extrapolation beyond the data range is a routine and consequential misuse.

name: discretisation of a continuous problem
essential_semantics: Replacing a continuous object by a finite one, with the discretisation parameter and the induced error explicit, and the continuous problem still represented.
canonical_example: replacing d/dx by a finite difference with step h
rationale: Discretisation is the paradigmatic lossy translation; whether the loss is recorded is the discriminating question.

name: grid or mesh over a domain
essential_semantics: A finite set of points or cells covering a domain, with resolution and boundary handling as parameters.
canonical_example: a uniform grid with spacing h on [0, L]
rationale: Mesh resolution is a stated approximation parameter with a direct effect on error.

name: time integration scheme and stability condition
essential_semantics: Explicit or implicit schemes with step size and stability restrictions (e.g. CFL) attached.
canonical_example: forward Euler with dt below the stability limit
rationale: The stability condition is a constraint on the numerical method that has no analogue in the continuous statement and must be surfaced.

name: algorithmic differentiation
essential_semantics: Exact-to-rounding derivatives of a program, distinguished from symbolic differentiation and from finite differences, with mode (forward/reverse) and differentiability preconditions.
canonical_example: reverse-mode gradient of a scalar loss over n parameters
rationale: AD silently returns a one-sided value at non-differentiable points; this is a real correctness gap worth representing.

name: finite-difference approximation of derivatives
essential_semantics: Difference quotient with a step size, carrying both truncation and rounding error, explicitly approximate.
canonical_example: (f(x+h) - f(x))/h approximates f'(x) with error O(h)
rationale: It is the canonical case where two error sources trade off, requiring the approximation to be explicit.

name: Monte Carlo estimation
essential_semantics: Estimating an expectation by sampling, with sample size, the resulting stochastic error, and the estimator's randomness explicit.
canonical_example: Ehat = (1/N) sum f(X_i) with standard error sigma/sqrt(N)
rationale: A Monte Carlo estimate is a random variable, not a number; representing it as a number hides its variability.

name: pseudo-random generation and seeding
essential_semantics: Randomness is produced by a named generator with a seed; a pseudo-random draw is not a mathematical random variable.
canonical_example: results reproducible given generator and seed
rationale: The mathematical model of randomness and its computational simulation are different objects and both should be nameable.

name: reproducibility conditions of a computed result
essential_semantics: The set of conditions (precision, seed, ordering, library version) under which a numeric result is reproducible, recorded with the result.
canonical_example: parallel reduction order changes the last bits of a sum
rationale: A numeric claim without reproducibility conditions cannot be verified by anyone else.

name: interval and validated arithmetic
essential_semantics: Computing with enclosures that provably contain the true value, at the cost of width growth.
canonical_example: [1.99, 2.01] contains the true value
rationale: It is the constructive counterpart to error bounds and shows that rigour is achievable numerically.

name: approximation as a first-class relation
essential_semantics: 'approximately equal' is a distinct relation from equality, carrying an error magnitude or bound, and is not transitive without accounting.
canonical_example: pi ≈ 3.1416 with error below 1e-4
rationale: Writing '=' where only '≈' holds is the most common way a computational representation overstates what it knows, and chained approximations accumulate error that must be tracked.

name: separation of exact and numeric evaluation paths
essential_semantics: The system distinguishes symbolic/exact evaluation from numeric evaluation and does not silently substitute one for the other.
canonical_example: sqrt(2) stays exact unless numeric evaluation is requested
rationale: Premature numeric evaluation destroys the ability to reason symbolically and silently introduces error.

name: sparsity and structural zeros
essential_semantics: A structural zero (known to be zero by the model) is distinct from a numerically small value, and sparsity patterns are part of the object.
canonical_example: a banded matrix whose off-band entries are structurally zero
rationale: The structural/numerical zero distinction affects both algorithms and model interpretation.

name: cost of evaluating a mathematical object
essential_semantics: The computational cost of evaluating an expression, distinguished from the mathematical content of the expression itself.
canonical_example: the determinant is defined combinatorially but computed by factorisation
rationale: Keeping definition and evaluation strategy separate is what allows one statement to have several implementations.
